channel.title: Deepgrain Intelligence
channel.description: Long-form essays on operating systems, AI readiness, and the craft of operating leadership.

item.title: The quiet discipline of operating leadership
item.description: The best operating leaders are quiet on the outside and rigorous on the inside. The volume is misleading.

item.title: Hiring for the grain: building teams that compound
item.description: The best hires don't fight the grain or surrender to it. They read it and add to it.

item.title: What CTOs get wrong about scale
item.description: Scale is rarely a technology problem. It is almost always an operating problem dressed up as a technology problem.

item.title: Founder-mode vs operator-mode
item.description: Founder-mode and operator-mode aren't opposites. They're alternating muscles. Knowing which to use, when, is the executive job.

item.title: The craft mindset for modern operators
item.description: Operating leadership is a craft. Crafts have masters, apprentices, tools, and standards. Most companies forget all four.

item.title: Operating consultancy for AI-native companies
item.description: AI-native companies have a different grain. The operating system has to assume agents, not just employees.

item.title: Operating consultancy for climate ventures
item.description: Climate ventures need to compound on a planetary timeline and a venture-fund clock at the same time.

item.title: Operating consultancy for transit and mobility
item.description: Transit organisations operate on the seam between hardware, software, and public trust. The grain runs in three directions at once.

item.title: The People Ops diagnostic toolkit
item.description: Five working diagnostics for People leaders: the underperformance early warning, the People-as-a-product checklist, the 90-day roadmap, the workflow heatmap, and the AI-readiness read. Use them together, not in isolation.

item.title: People debt: what GenAI exposes, and what to do about it
item.description: GenAI does not create People debt. It exposes it. Inconsistent levelling, undocumented processes, decision rights nobody can name, all become legible the moment you try to automate around them. The audit, and the order to repay.

item.title: Designing values that stick
item.description: Most corporate values projects fail. They produce a poster, not a behaviour. The values that actually shape a company are short, specific, costly to live by, and wired into how decisions get made. Here is the design pattern.

item.title: Coaching and feedback systems that actually compound
item.description: Most performance systems run once a quarter and decay between cycles. The systems that compound are weekly, lightweight, evidence-led, and instrumented. Here is the operating shape that works, and where AI fits without flattening the craft.

item.title: AI roadmap case study: FinEdge's first 90 days
item.description: How a 280-person fintech People team went from scattered ChatGPT use to nine production workflows in 90 days. The exact sequence, the trade-offs, the metrics, and the two near-misses.

item.title: Operating consultancy for financial data
item.description: Financial data businesses are operating systems wearing product clothing. Treat the substrate as the product.

item.title: The HR Architect: a new role inside the People function
item.description: Every white-collar job is a sequence of clicks. AI is starting at the click layer and moving up. The roles that survive are the ones that change shape: from operator to architect.

item.title: The automation audit playbook
item.description: Most automation efforts fail because they start with "what can I automate?" The right question is "what problems am I trying to solve?" A problem-first audit, with the 6T framework and a prioritisation matrix.

item.title: An AI policy blueprint for People teams
item.description: An AI policy that enables, not strangles. Foundational prep, governance, guardrails, and how to handle shadow AI without driving it deeper underground.

item.title: Production agents for People Ops
item.description: Most "agents" in People Ops are demos with ambition. The ones that survive contact with production share a pattern: data first, structured context, exception handling, observability, human escalation.

item.title: An AI enablement operating model for People leaders
item.description: Champions are a distribution layer, not a strategy. The operating model that makes AI enablement compound has three connected layers: org-wide, team-wide, individual.

item.title: Operating consultancy for defence tech
item.description: Defence tech runs on dual mandates: warfighter outcomes and commercial scale. The operating system has to hold both.

item.title: Choosing AI models for HR work
item.description: A practical guide to which AI model to reach for by HR task type. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, and the trade-offs that actually matter when the work is real.

item.title: Prompting patterns for People Ops
item.description: A working library of prompt patterns for People teams: the five building blocks, prompt chaining, critical-thinking prompts that stress-test your output, and the model-specific shifts you need for GPT-5 and Claude class models.

item.title: What good looks like: signals of operating health
item.description: Operating health doesn't show up in the dashboard. It shows up in how an org talks about its own mistakes.

item.title: AI workspace setup for People teams (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot)
item.description: How to set up an AI workspace for a People team: custom instructions, projects, and reference documents that turn AI from a search bar into a colleague. Works for Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini.

item.title: From prompts to systems
item.description: Most People teams are stuck between dabbling and tool-shopping. The third path is building. It has a grain, and it has a mechanic: workflows, automations, agents, in that order.

item.title: Designing the AI-native People team
item.description: Most People functions bolt AI onto the existing org chart. The ones pulling ahead redesign around it — different roles, different ratios, different leverage. Here is what an AI-native People team actually looks like.

item.title: AI governance for People teams
item.description: Governance is not the brake. It is the steering. The People teams that stay fast with AI are the ones that decided early what they would never let it decide.

item.title: The champion model
item.description: You don't need engineers to build AI capability inside the People function. You need three or four champions, given air cover and time. Here is how the model actually works.

item.title: Leading the AI transformation in People
item.description: AI in People Ops fails as a change programme more often than as a technology problem. Here is the operating playbook for leading the transformation without losing the team.

item.title: Diagnosing AI readiness in People Ops
item.description: A two-axis maturity read plus a six-axis diagnostic for People functions. Use it before you build anything, so you build the right thing first.

item.title: A workflow assessment framework for People Ops
item.description: Most People teams pick AI workflows by instinct or by what is loudest. A simple scoring framework — value, frequency, fit, risk — turns a wishlist into a 90-day plan you can actually defend.

item.title: Automation patterns that pay off
item.description: Six concrete workflow patterns we keep seeing work inside People functions. Built with n8n, an LLM, and a champion. Live in weeks, not quarters.

item.title: The People Ops AI domain map
item.description: A map of where AI fits across the People function — from sourcing to offboarding — so you can see the whole estate before you build any one piece of it.

item.title: Measuring AI value in People Ops
item.description: If the CFO asks what your AI investment has returned, vague time-saving stories are not enough. Here is how to measure People Ops AI value properly — and tell the story to a board that knows the difference.

item.title: Scaling without breaking the grain
item.description: Most companies break themselves at scale. The ones that don't are the ones that scaled with the grain, not against it.

item.title: The art of the operating intervention
item.description: An intervention is the smallest change that produces the largest second-order effect. The craft is in the smallness.

item.title: How to diagnose an organisation in 30 days
item.description: A 30-day diagnostic protocol: who to listen to, what to look for, and the trap of premature recommendations.

item.title: Read · Craft · Scale: the Deepgrain method
item.description: Three movements, in order. Skip the first and the rest is theatre. Skip the third and the work doesn't compound.

item.title: The AI operating ladder: five tiers explained
item.description: From ad-hoc usage to autonomous operations: the five tiers of AI operating maturity, what each one looks like in practice, and what it takes to climb each rung.

item.title: From AI experiments to AI infrastructure
item.description: Experiments are cheap. Infrastructure is expensive. The companies that win the next decade are the ones that know when to switch, and what to switch into.

item.title: Why AI pilots stall at production
item.description: The path from pilot to production is paved with the things nobody wanted to think about during the demo. Here is the recurring pattern, and how to design pilots that actually cross it.

item.title: The five pillars of AI readiness
item.description: Readiness is not a model selection problem. It is a Data, Tools, Agents, Governance, and Cadence problem, in that order. Here is the diagnostic, with what good and bad look like at each pillar.

item.title: What is an AI operating system? (AI OS, explained)
item.description: An AI operating system, or AI OS, is the layer between models and work. It is what turns a clever demo into a compounding capability. Here is what it includes, how it differs from an operating model, and how to build one.

item.title: The difference between strategy and operating reality
item.description: Strategy is a story about the future. Operating reality is a description of the present. Most leadership teams confuse the two.

item.title: Operating systems vs operating models
item.description: An operating model is a slide. An operating system is what runs when nobody is looking. The distinction is the entire point.

item.title: The grain metaphor: reading your organisation
item.description: Wood has a grain. So does every organisation. Cut with it and the work compounds; cut against it and you spend the rest of the year sanding.

item.title: Why most change programmes fail
item.description: 70% of change programmes fail. The reason is rarely strategy — it's that the grain was never read before the cut was made.

item.title: What is organisational consultancy?
item.description: Organisational consultancy is the practice of reading how a company actually operates — and changing it without breaking what works.
